text: In December of eighteen fifty-nine, settlers founded a cotton town on the Virgin River, part of a southern Utah project ordered by Brigham Young.
They called it Wheeler. Then, on the night of January eighth, eighteen sixty-two, the river flooded.
The Great Flood of eighteen sixty-two largely destroyed the settlement.
The survivors rebuilt about a mile upriver, and named the new town Grafton.
Seven years after its founding, fear of attack during the Black Hawk War emptied the town completely.
Every resident was evacuated to nearby Rockville, and the town stood empty.
Grafton filled again. The census counted one hundred six residents in nineteen ten, the most it ever recorded.
That remains the highest count on record.
Grafton faded slowly. Its local church branch was discontinued in nineteen twenty-one.
By the mid nineteen forties, almost everyone had gone.
Hollywood later used the empty town as a film location, including Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid.
Since nineteen ninety-seven, the Grafton Heritage Partnership has worked to protect and restore it.
When Grafton was evacuated in eighteen sixty-six, its families went to nearby Rockville.
Rockville still has a red sandstone house with a small office addition that held a telegraph and a post office.
The main building is two stories, with a low second floor.
The National Register of Historic Places listed the Deseret Telegraph and Post Office in nineteen seventy-two.
In the fall of eighteen sixty-two, settlers answering a call to grow cotton settled at the mouth of Zion Canyon.
Local lore says the name came from a settler's wife, who looked at the big springs beside their home and called it Springdale.
It stayed a farming town until after nineteen hundred.
Around nineteen twelve, the first automobile drove in.
Grafton, Utah. Settled in eighteen fifty-nine. Flooded in eighteen sixty-two. Evacuated in eighteen sixty-six.
Its census peak came in nineteen ten, with one hundred six people.
By the mid nineteen forties, almost everyone had gone.
By nineteen seventeen, tourists from as far away as Salt Lake City were staying at Wylie Way Camp.
It was one of the first tourist facilities near Zion.
In nineteen thirty, the Zion Mount Carmel Highway and Tunnel was dedicated, bringing the town its first highway access from the east.
A cotton town beside Zion, now a ghost town.
